title: Table, pulpit, font
hook: where the furniture sits says what's central

segments.voice: Yesterday, domes: a round roof painted as the heavens, with Christ Pantocrator looking down. Your line was heaven overhead. Who was under the same roof with you yesterday? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-six.

A table. A pulpit. A font. Look around inside a church and those three keep turning up. In one church, the table stands in the middle at the front, candles on it, and the pulpit waits off to one side. In another, a tall pulpit rises dead center, a big Bible open on it, and the table sits lower down, in front. In a third, behind the pulpit, set high into the wall where everyone can see it, there's a pool of water deep enough to stand in. Same three pieces of furniture. Three different arrangements. And none of them got there by accident. Today: table, pulpit, font.

Jesus says, "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." A church's floor plan is a little like that. Where the furniture stands shows what the people treasure in their worship. Start with the table. At the last supper, Jesus took bread and said, "This do in remembrance of me." Paul calls it "the Lord's table." Catholic Christians call it an altar, Orthodox Christians the holy table or altar, and they place it at the heart of the church, because they understand the Eucharist celebrated there as the center of their worship. Some Lutheran and Anglican churches do the same. Next, the pulpit. Paul writes, "So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God." In Reformed and Presbyterian churches, the pulpit may stand at the center, with the Bible open on it, because the word read and preached is where they hear God speak. The table is still there, and honored, but the eye goes first to the open book. Then, the font. Water for baptism. In some Baptist churches the baptistry, a pool for full immersion, is set up high behind the pulpit, so that every baptism happens in front of the whole room. Tomorrow we'll stand by the font. Last, put them together. Some churches set all three in a line, or in a triangle, so all three are held together. Every arrangement is an answer to the same question, made in wood and stone instead of words. Christians don't all give the same answer. And each answer can be read from the back pew.

Here's the practice: notice what's central in your home. Settle where you are, and breathe. Then let your eyes move around the room without judging anything. What stands in the middle? What do the chairs face? A table, a screen, a window, a bed? Rest your eyes on that center for a while. If you pray, you can hold Jesus's words in mind: where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. Or simply sit with the room as it is, and notice what it has been built around. The bell holds the time.
screen: `WHERE YOUR TREASURE IS, THERE WILL YOUR HEART BE ALSO.`

segments.voice: Table. The Lord's table, the altar at the heart of a church; with the pulpit and the font, one of three pieces whose places show what a church puts first.

Your line: what's at the center. Today, sit once at a table in your home with nothing else going on, no phone, no screen, and notice what it's like to make that the center for a few minutes. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-six.

fork.setup: you're helping plan a church for people who believe faith comes by hearing the word of God. what goes dead center?
options: the pulpit, with the Bible open on it
fork.reveal: Reformed and Presbyterian churches may center the pulpit for just that reason: "faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God."

original.note: Greek: table. Paul's word in 1 Corinthians 10:21, "the Lord's table."

trapdoor: what you thought: church furniture is just furniture.
what it means: where the table, pulpit and font stand shows what a church puts at its center.
what a scholar hears: Paul's phrase "the Lord's table": one piece of furniture, which some churches call an altar and others a table.

notes: Word is 'Table' per the index (title head). Script teaches all three pieces; the word segment centers the table.
'Some Lutheran and Anglican churches do the same' (altar at the center): confirm.
Reformed/Presbyterian centered pulpit and Baptist baptistry behind the pulpit are stated with 'may' / 'some'; confirm fair.
Catholic and Orthodox understanding of the Eucharist as 'the center of everything' is a paraphrase of their teaching; confirm wording.
Luke 22:19 setting given as 'at a table on the night before he died'; confirm acceptable.
